standard.title: Locate, select and analyse information
standard.description: locate, select and analyse information and data from a range of sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can locate, select and analyse information and data from a range of sources at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S02). They have practised searching for economic information, evaluating sources for relevance and reliability, and using digital tools to organise data. Y10 builds on this with more complex sources, more contextually specific search strategies, and explicit attention to assumptions and missing information in sources.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate, select and analyse economic and business information and data from a range of sources, evaluating relevance, reliability and the assumptions or gaps that may affect interpretation.

nodes.label: Locating sources using contextually specific search
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use contextually specific search strategies to locate relevant economic and business sources, including using appropriate terminology and criteria.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two contextually specific search terms or criteria (e.g. 'global markets', 'trade agreements Australia case studies') to locate sources relevant to an inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Locate online sources using contextually specific terms (e.g. 'global markets', 'fiscal policy Australia 2024') and criteria (e.g. key words to find 'case studies related to trade agreements'); explain how search strategy affects the quality and relevance of sources found.
wider: Compare the results of searching the same topic using a general search engine vs an academic database or government statistical portal and evaluate the difference in source quality
Develop a search protocol for a complex economic inquiry — including Boolean operators, date filters and domain restrictions — and evaluate what the protocol is designed to achieve
Investigate how algorithmic filtering in online search affects what economic information people find and evaluate implications for informed decision-making

response_modes.reason: Practise the search strategy move across multiple economic topics. Students need to internalise the connection between inquiry question → relevant search terms → source quality before they can reliably find usable sources.

success_criteria: Uses at least two contextually specific search terms derived from the inquiry question
Locates at least two sources that are relevant to the inquiry question

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for relevance and reliability
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate economic information and data sources for relevance and reliability, using explicit criteria including who collected the data, when, and for what purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least two relevance or reliability criteria to evaluate a provided economic source.
nodes.typical_width: Select and analyse economic information and data for relevance (asking: How will this help answer the inquiry question?) and reliability (asking: How and when was the data collected? Who collected it? For what purpose?); explain assumptions or missing information that may affect reliability.
wider: Compare two sources presenting conflicting economic data on the same issue (e.g. different unemployment measures) and evaluate which is more reliable for a specific inquiry purpose
Investigate how government statistical agencies (ABS) and advocacy groups may present different data on the same economic phenomenon and explain how purpose shapes data collection and presentation
Evaluate a secondary source (news article, commentary) against its primary data source and identify what has been changed, emphasised or omitted in the reporting
nodes.hinge_reason: The reliability evaluation move is what the descriptor's 'analyse' demand requires. Students who accept sources uncritically cannot complete the inquiry work the descriptor specifies — their findings will be built on unstated assumptions or unreliable data.

response_modes.reason: Make the evaluation criteria explicit and practise applying them to real economic sources. Students commonly evaluate 'quality' vaguely — the structured criteria (who, when, purpose, assumptions) need to become habitual.

Apply reliability evaluation to different source types — ABS data, Reserve Bank reports, media articles, advocacy group reports — so students develop differentiated criteria rather than applying the same checklist uniformly.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Contrasting source types (statistical authority vs advocacy, primary vs secondary) provides rich material for developing critical information literacy. The ability to identify assumptions and missing information is a high-demand skill that rewards wide application.
success_criteria: Applies at least two named criteria to evaluate a source's relevance or reliability
Identifies at least one assumption or missing information in a source that could affect its reliability

nodes.label: Representing and using information with digital tools
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and represent economic information using specialised digital tools to support interpretation and analysis of an inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent economic information in at least one organised format (e.g. table, graphic organiser, annotated chart) that supports interpretation of the inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Select and represent information and data about an economic or business issue using specialised digital tools and processes to support interpretation and analysis — for example, a graphic organiser connecting government economic objectives with examples of intervention; an annotated data table showing trends.
wider: Use data visualisation tools (e.g. Canva, Datawrapper, spreadsheet charting) to represent and interpret economic trend data, explaining what the representation reveals that raw data does not
Design a multi-source synthesis document that represents economic information from three or more sources in a way that enables comparison and analysis
Evaluate the representational choices in an existing economic infographic or data dashboard and assess what those choices emphasise or obscure

response_modes.reason: Apply digital representation to varied data types — trend data, comparative data, causal relationship data — so students develop flexible tool use rather than competence with only one format.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Digital tool proficiency for economic data representation is both practically useful and intellectually rewarding — learning to make representational choices develops meta-cognitive awareness of how data presentation shapes interpretation.
success_criteria: Represents economic information in an organised format that is connected to the inquiry question
Explains how the representation supports analysis (what it makes visible or easier to compare)
